introduction: The Budapest Museum of Illusions is a branch of a franchise that began in Croatia in 2015. The Budapest venue near Deák Square was reported as newly opened in December 2021, and 2026 reports describe a closure and a renovated version.
chapters: A Croatian idea becomes a franchise

According to Wikipedia, the Museum of Illusions was founded by Tomislav Pamuković and Roko Živković. The founders say the idea came from contemplating how to escape the corporate environment, and the article says it was inspired by the National Geographic show Brain Games. The first museum opened in 2015 in Zagreb, Croatia, after two years between idea and realisation. Franchising began in 2016 with museums in Zadar, Croatia, and Ljubljana, Slovenia. As of May 2023, the franchise had 43 museums in 25 countries, according to the same article.
The Budapest branch of 2021

A We Love Budapest article published on 9 December 2021 described the Budapest museum as newly opened, at Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út 3, near Deák tér in downtown Budapest. It reported optical illusion rooms that make visitors look huge or tiny, or appear upside down, and a main attraction in the form of a tunnel that creates the impression the whole world is moving. The same report said the franchise had operations in Zadar and Zagreb and, in the writer's words, more than 50 major cities, and noted that the article may contain outdated information.
Reports of a closure and a renovated museum

A Budappest news item dated 28 July 2026 said the museum would close in its current form on 24 August 2026 and return later in a brand-new, more modern version, giving no reopening date and no reason. A Hungary Unlocked guide with an update date of 20 October 2026 describes the museum as reopened after a renovation. The two sources do not give a shared timeline, so the current status should be confirmed on the museum's official channels.

introduction: The Fradi Museum tells the story of Ferencvárosi Torna Club, founded in 1899 in Budapest's ninth district. It now sits inside the club's arena, which replaced the older Albert Flórián stadium in 2014.
chapters: Founding in the ninth district

Wikipedia says Ferencvárosi Torna Club was founded on 3 May 1899 by Ferenc Springer and a group of residents of Budapest's ninth district, Ferencváros. The club's colours are green and white, and the nine stripes on the badge, five green and four white, represent the district. The nickname Fradi comes from Franzstadt, the German name for the area. The club's earlier home was the Üllői út stadium, where it had played since 1911; it was later known as Stadion Albert Flórián and was demolished in 2013.
Re-founding, European finals and the Fairs Cup

A review of the museum says its 1950s room features a 1956 radio recording announcing the club's re-founding, after the communist regime had renamed the club, changed its colours and recruited its best players. Wikipedia records the club's 1964-65 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup win, in which it beat Juventus 1-0 in Turin in the final. It lost the 1968 Fairs Cup final to Leeds United and the 1975 European Cup Winners' Cup final to Dynamo Kyiv. In 1995-96 it was the first Hungarian club to qualify for the renewed Champions League.
A new arena and a museum of its own

Wikipedia says the old stadium was demolished in 2013 and the new one was built on its site, with construction in 2013 and 2014. It was designed by Ágnes Streit and Szabolcs Kormos and opened on 10 August 2014 with a match against Chelsea. The Fradi Museum is inside the stadium. Wikipedia says it opened on 7 August 2014, while a 2015 review says it existed for decades but received official museum status in 2015 when it moved into the new arena. Sources therefore differ on the exact year.

introduction: The National Dance Theatre's story runs through two very different buildings: the former Carmelite church in Buda Castle, which was a theatre from the 1780s, and a converted factory at Millenáris Park, which opened in 2019.
chapters: From Carmelite church to Castle Theatre

Wikipedia says the site first held a Franciscan church of St John, built in 1269-1270, which became a mosque under Ottoman rule and was destroyed in the 1686 siege of Buda. The Carmelites received the plot in 1693, laid the foundation stone in 1725 and finished the church by 1736. After Emperor Joseph II dissolved the order in 1784, the church was converted into the Castle Theatre in 1786 to plans by Wolfgang von Kempelen, with the high altar turned into the stage. The first play in Hungarian was staged there on 25 October 1790.
War damage, closure and the Várszínház

The theatre reopened in 1918 but closed in 1924 after a gallery collapsed, and it remained shut for about five decades, according to Wikipedia. Bombing in the Second World War damaged the building and collapsed the balcony, and it was renovated in 1947. It reopened on 13 February 1978 as the Várszínház. It housed the Népszínház until 1982 and then served as the National Theatre's chamber theatre until 1 December 2001. A Hungarian account says the National Dance Theatre began operating in the building on that date.
Leaving the Castle for Millenáris

Sources disagree about when the dance theatre left the Castle building: one 2019 report says it was based there from 2001 to 2014, while Wikipedia says the building was the theatre's home from 2001 to 2019 and that the government took it over in 2014 before the Prime Minister's office moved in during 2019. A 2019 news report said the theatre had to leave so that the prime minister could work from the Castle. The new building in Millenáris Park, at Kis Rókus utca 16-20, opened on 15 February 2019 according to the theatre's own site. It occupies a converted former factory from the Ganz works.

introduction: Müpa Budapest was built between 2002 and 2005 as the Palace of Arts, with a concert hall, a theatre and a museum built in parallel. It was renamed Müpa Budapest in 2015.
chapters: Building a cultural complex in 2002-2005

Wikipedia says the Palace of Arts was built from 2002 to 2005 to designs by Zoboki, Demeter and Partners, with the general contractors Trigránit and Arcadom Építőipari Zrt. The concert hall, the Festival Theatre and the Ludwig Museum were built in parallel over 28 months. The building has about 10,000 square metres of ground area and 70,000 square metres of floor space. It stands in Ferencváros near Rákóczi Bridge, next to the National Theatre, which opened in 2002, and both are part of the Millennium City Center development.
The opening and the organ

The complex was officially opened on 14 March 2005. Its Béla Bartók National Concert Hall has acoustics designed by Russell Johnson, adjustable with 58 movable resonance chambers and a suspended 42-tonne canopy. The hall's organ was inaugurated on 22 May 2006. It has 92 stops, 5 manuals and about 6,700 pipes and was built by Orgelbau Mühleisen with the Pécs Organ Building Manufactory. Wikipedia says the complex won the FIABCI Prix d'Excellence in 2006 and the FIABCI audience award in 2007.
From Palace of Arts to Müpa

Between 2005 and 2015 the building was known as the Palace of Arts, and it was then renamed Müpa Budapest. The Ludwig Museum, a museum of contemporary art, occupies the Danube-facing side and was previously housed in Buda Castle, according to its own website. The Festival Theatre, in the east wing, seats 452, and the main lobby connects the three main parts of the complex.

introduction: The Budapest Music Center began as an organisation in 1996 and moved into its own converted building at Mátyás utca 8 in 2013. That building began as a one-storey neoclassical residential house built in 1890.
chapters: An organisation founded in 1996

BMC's own about page says it was founded in 1996 by trombonist and former academy professor László Gőz. Its aim was to present contemporary Hungarian music in a collective and coordinated way. BMC works as a concert promoter, a record label and an information centre. Its record label, BMC Records, was founded in 1998, and BMC's site says it has released more than 370 albums in classical, contemporary and jazz music on CD and in digital formats.
From an 1890 house to a music centre

A Graphisoft case study says the building began as a one-storey neoclassical residential building from 1890, with shops on the ground floor facing the street. Preparation, design and implementation took close to 10 years, and most of the transformation was financed from private resources. The centre opened in spring 2013. The architects were Art1st Design Studio. The original elevations were conserved and refurbished, the entrance was moved to the street corner, and the concert hall was built in the former inner courtyard with its exposed brick walls kept.
The centre since 2013

BMC says the building houses a concert hall, the Opus Jazz Club, the music library, BMC Records and the Peter Eötvös Contemporary Music Foundation. The Opus Jazz Club also opened in 2013. Since 2014 the information centre and library has published monographs on Hungarian composers. The Graphisoft case study adds that the founder issued a written statement forbidding future owners from changing the building's content or function, or selling or transforming it.

introduction: The Hungarian Heritage House was established in 2001 in the Budai Vigadó, a Buda entertainment hall built in 1898-1900. It draws on the dance house movement that began in Budapest in 1972 and on the Hungarian State Folk Ensemble founded in the early 1950s.
chapters: The Buda Vigadó of 1898-1900

The Heritage House's own page says its building was the historic Vigadó, an entertainment hall, of Buda. It was built between 1898 and 1900 by Aladár Árkay and Mór Kallina as a cultural complex for Buda's middle class, with a theatre, library, cafe and restaurant. The exterior is eclectic with a relatively simple facade, while the interior has rich Art Nouveau ornamentation, including a columned hall with a wide marble staircase. The page does not describe the building's later history or restoration, so those details should be checked separately.
Dance houses and a state folk ensemble

The Heritage House's page on its dance house says the first Budapest dance house was held in May 1972, based on the experience of the dance houses of Szék in Transylvania. Wikipedia adds that in November 2011 UNESCO recognised the táncház method as a way of reviving and safeguarding traditional dance teaching. The Hungarian State Folk Ensemble is described as the first professional folk dance ensemble in Hungary. Miklós Rábai was chosen in 1950 to establish its dance chorus, and its inaugural performance, with the Moiseyev Ensemble, took place on 4 April 1951 at the Opera House.
An institute founded in 2001

The Hungarian Heritage House was established in 2001 as an institute of national significance based in the Budai Vigadó on Corvin Square. Its mission is to preserve folk traditions of the Carpathian Basin and bring back small cultural elements that have faded or are fading. A February 2021 report said the institute marked 20 years in 2021, a double jubilee with the 70th anniversary of the Folk Ensemble, which also works from the building. Its activities include stage folk dance, handicraft classes, archiving of folklore footage and folk arts education.
